title: Preconception health, nutrition and supplements
blurb: Give current NICE NG247 advice on folic acid, vitamin D, weight, Healthy Start and food safety before and during pregnancy.
question: Leila, 31, has type 2 diabetes and a BMI of 33. She is planning a pregnancy and asks which supplements she should take and at what dose. What should the midwife advise?

teach.body: Formally, NICE NG247 (January 2025) advises folic acid before conception and in early pregnancy, vitamin D during pregnancy and breastfeeding, healthy eating and activity, and sensitive weight management, with information in a person's preferred format. In plain English: the right supplement at the right dose, from before conception, prevents serious harm such as neural tube defects, and good nutrition advice must be practical, affordable and free of judgement.

teach.text: Older teaching gave 5 mg to women with a BMI of 30 or more. NG247 (2025) reassures anyone with a BMI of 25 or more, or at increased risk of pre-eclampsia, that 400 micrograms is enough unless a 1.1.5 risk factor applies. Diabetes (type 1 or 2) IS a 5 mg factor.

teach.h: Healthy Start and vitamins to avoid
teach.body: Healthy Start vitamins for pregnant or breastfeeding women contain 400 micrograms folic acid plus vitamins C and D, free to those eligible; children's drops contain vitamins A, C and D until the fourth birthday. In pregnancy do not take cod liver oil or supplements containing vitamin A (retinol), which may include ordinary multivitamins. On a vegan or restricted diet, add vitamin B12 foods or a supplement.

Offer to measure height and weight at the first face-to-face appointment and explain why (NG247 1.2.7). Share BMI sensitively, for example written down rather than spoken, or not at all if she prefers (1.2.8). BMI 30+: offer gestational diabetes testing; BMI 40+: discuss specialist referral. Do not weigh routinely without a clinical reason, and advise against intentional weight loss in pregnancy. No need to 'eat for two'.

teach.body: Midwife Sara advises Leila to take 5 mg folic acid daily from now until 12 weeks of pregnancy, because type 2 diabetes is a high-dose risk factor, not because of her BMI. She advises vitamin D 10 micrograms daily, explains Healthy Start eligibility, warns against cod liver oil and vitamin A supplements, and explains that alcohol is best avoided. She discusses healthy eating and activity without blame and links Leila with her diabetes team.

items: Folic acid 400 micrograms, ideally 3 months before conception to 12 weeks, even with fortified flour.
5 mg for NTD history, previous affected pregnancy, diabetes, sickle cell or thalassaemia, anti-epileptic or HIV medicines.
BMI alone or pre-eclampsia risk alone does not need 5 mg.
Vitamin D 10 micrograms October to March, all year with darker skin or little sun; avoid vitamin A.
Weigh sensitively at booking, no routine weighing, no dieting in pregnancy; know food-safety basics.

summary: You can now give current NICE NG247 advice on folic acid dose and duration, high-dose indications, vitamin D and Healthy Start, and handle weight sensitively. You can also give practical food-safety, alcohol and caffeine advice.

A.q: Emma, 28, has no medical conditions and is planning her first pregnancy. What folic acid advice should the midwife give?
options: 400 micrograms daily, from 3 months before until 12 weeks
5 mg daily from conception until the baby is born
400 micrograms daily, starting from the 12-week scan
None needed, as UK flour is now fortified with it
A.why: NG247 1.1.3-1.1.4: 400 micrograms a day, ideally for 3 months before trying to conceive and for at least the first 12 weeks.

whyNot.1: 5 mg is for specific risk factors and is advised to 12 weeks, not to birth.
whyNot.2: Starting at 12 weeks misses the period when the neural tube forms.
whyNot.3: NG247 says take folic acid even if food is fortified.

A.q: Which woman planning a pregnancy should be offered 5 mg folic acid a day under NICE NG247?
options: Amira, BMI 34, with no other risk factors
Beth, who had pre-eclampsia last pregnancy
Chiara, who has type 1 diabetes
Dee, aged 41, with no medical history
A.why: NG247 1.1.5: type 1 or type 2 diabetes is a high-dose indication.

whyNot.0: BMI of 25 or more alone does not need more than 400 micrograms (1.1.6).
whyNot.1: Increased risk of pre-eclampsia alone does not need more than 400 micrograms (1.1.7).
whyNot.3: Age is not a 1.1.5 risk factor.

A.q: What daily dose of vitamin D does NICE NG247 recommend for pregnant and breastfeeding women?
options: 10 micrograms (400 IU)
25 micrograms (1,000 IU)
100 micrograms (4,000 IU)
1 microgram (40 IU)
A.why: NG247 1.1.12: 10 micrograms (400 IU) a day, October to March, or all year if at increased risk of deficiency.

whyNot.1: 25 micrograms is not the NG247 dose.
whyNot.2: 100 micrograms is far above the recommended daily dose.
whyNot.3: 1 microgram is far below the recommended dose.

B.q: Hana, whose family is of south Asian origin and who covers most of her skin outdoors, asks when to take vitamin D in pregnancy. What should the midwife advise?
options: October to March, like all women
In the third trimester
When she starts breastfeeding
Throughout the year
B.why: NG247 1.1.12: take 10 micrograms all year if at increased risk of deficiency, for example darker skin or little sun exposure.

whyNot.0: October to March applies to women without extra risk factors.
whyNot.1: Vitamin D is advised throughout pregnancy, not one trimester.
whyNot.2: It is needed in pregnancy as well as when breastfeeding.

B.q: At 10 weeks, Jo says she takes cod liver oil capsules every day because 'they're good for the baby's brain'. What should the midwife advise?
options: Continue, as fish oils support brain growth
Halve the dose until after 20 weeks
Stop, as they contain vitamin A
Switch to a standard multivitamin
B.why: NG247 1.1.12: during pregnancy do not take cod liver oil or supplements containing vitamin A (retinol).

whyNot.0: Cod liver oil contains vitamin A, which can harm the baby.
whyNot.1: A lower dose still contains vitamin A; NICE advises not taking it.
whyNot.3: Regular multivitamins may contain retinol; choose a pregnancy-specific or Healthy Start product.

B.q: At booking, Mia says she finds being weighed upsetting and does not want to hear her BMI. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Skip height and weight for the whole pregnancy
Weigh her at each visit to build her confidence
Explain she must lose weight during pregnancy
Explain why it matters and share it as she prefers
B.why: NG247 1.2.7-1.2.8: offer to measure at booking and explain why; reassure her that weight and BMI can be shared sensitively, such as written down, or not shared, as she prefers.

whyNot.0: Booking BMI informs care planning, so it should be offered with an explanation.
whyNot.1: NICE advises against routine weighing without a clinical reason.
whyNot.2: Intentional weight loss in pregnancy is not recommended.

C.q: Leila, 31, has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and a BMI of 33. She is planning a pregnancy. Which folic acid advice is correct?
options: 400 micrograms, as BMI no longer needs a high dose
5 mg until 12 weeks, because she has diabetes
5 mg until 12 weeks, because her BMI is over 30
Start folic acid once a pregnancy test is positive
C.why: NG247 1.1.5: diabetes (type 1 or 2) is a high-dose indication. Her BMI alone would not need 5 mg, but diabetes does.

whyNot.0: Correct about BMI, but it misses her diabetes, which needs 5 mg.
whyNot.2: BMI is no longer a reason for 5 mg under NG247 1.1.6.
whyNot.3: Folic acid should start before conception, ideally 3 months before.

C.q: Grace has a booking BMI of 42 and no other risk factors. Which plan best follows NICE NG247?
options: Advise a calorie-restricted diet to lose weight
Weigh her at every appointment to monitor gain
Prescribe 5 mg folic acid because of her BMI
Offer diabetes testing and discuss specialist referral
C.why: NG247 1.2.9-1.2.10: with BMI 30+ offer gestational diabetes testing; with BMI 40+ discuss referral to a specialist obesity service or practitioner.

whyNot.0: Intentional weight loss is not recommended in pregnancy (1.2.15).
whyNot.1: Routine weighing is not recommended without a clinical reason (1.2.13).
whyNot.2: BMI alone does not need more than 400 micrograms (1.1.6).

C.q: At 24 weeks, Sophie asks whether she can eat a baked camembert at a restaurant. What should the midwife advise, based on NHS food safety advice?
options: Yes, if it is cooked until steaming hot
Yes, cold, if it is made from pasteurised milk
No, all cheese should be avoided in pregnancy
Yes, if it is eaten before its use-by date
C.why: Mould-ripened soft cheeses such as camembert can contain listeria and must be thoroughly cooked until steaming hot.

whyNot.1: Mould-ripened soft cheeses need cooking whether pasteurised or not.
whyNot.2: Hard cheeses and pasteurised soft cheeses without a white rind are safe.
whyNot.3: The use-by date does not remove listeria risk in uncooked soft ripened cheese.

reteach.title: Dose, duration, and the 'not BMI' rule
reteach.question: Can you choose the right folic acid dose for five different women in under a minute?

blocks.body: Everyone: 400 micrograms from ideally 3 months before conception to 12 weeks. High dose 5 mg: a history of neural tube defects (her, partner or family), a previous affected pregnancy, diabetes, sickle cell or thalassaemia, or medicines such as anti-epileptics or HIV drugs. BMI and pre-eclampsia risk on their own: stay on 400 micrograms.

blocks.text: The high dose stops at 12 weeks, like the standard dose; it is not taken for the whole pregnancy.

explain.body: 400 micrograms daily, ideally 3 months before trying to conceive and for at least the first 12 weeks, even with fortified flour (NG247 1.1.3-1.1.4). 5 mg for the 1.1.5 risk factors. Explore barriers if she is not taking it (1.1.9).

test.q: Lou has epilepsy treated with an anti-epileptic medicine and is planning a pregnancy. What folic acid dose does NICE NG247 recommend?
options: 400 micrograms daily
1 mg daily
5 mg daily
800 micrograms daily
test.why: NG247 1.1.5: medicines that affect folic acid absorption or metabolism, such as anti-epileptics, are a high-dose (5 mg) indication.

whyNot.0: 400 micrograms is the standard dose, not for this risk factor.
whyNot.1: 1 mg is not an NG247 dose.
whyNot.3: 800 micrograms is not an NG247 dose.

explain.h: Vitamin D, Healthy Start, vitamin A
explain.body: Vitamin D 10 micrograms (400 IU) October to March, or all year with darker skin or little sun. Healthy Start: 400 micrograms folic acid plus vitamins C and D for pregnant and breastfeeding women; children's drops A, C and D. Avoid cod liver oil and retinol supplements in pregnancy.

test.q: A mother is formula feeding her 3-month-old with more than 500 mL of infant formula a day. Does the baby need a vitamin D supplement under NG247?
options: Yes, 8.5 to 10 micrograms a day
No, as the formula is fortified
Yes, starting at 6 months
Yes, 10 micrograms from October
test.why: NG247 table 1: babies taking 500 mL or more of formula a day do not need a supplement because formula is fortified.

whyNot.0: 8.5 to 10 micrograms is for breastfed babies.
whyNot.2: No supplement is needed while on 500 mL or more of formula.
whyNot.3: Seasonal timing is the adult rule; this baby needs none.

explain.body: No need to eat for two or follow a special diet, but eat a variety of foods. Measure at booking and share BMI sensitively. BMI 30+: offer GDM testing; 40+: discuss specialist referral. No routine weighing; no intentional weight loss. Stay active and limit sedentary time.

test.q: Priya asks if she should 'eat for two' now she is pregnant. What does NICE NG247 advise?
options: Yes, double her usual portions
No special diet, but eat a variety of foods
Yes, add 500 kcal a day from booking
No, she should reduce her intake to limit weight gain
test.why: NG247 1.2.2: reassure people they do not need to eat for two or follow a special diet, but should eat a variety of foods every day.

whyNot.0: NICE specifically addresses this myth: no eating for two.
whyNot.2: NG247 does not set an extra calorie target.
whyNot.3: Restricting intake to limit gain is not advised; focus on healthy diet and activity.

explain.body: Cook mould-ripened and soft blue cheeses until steaming hot; avoid unpasteurised milk, liver, raw or undercooked meat, and swordfish, shark and marlin; limit oily fish to 2 portions and tuna to 4 cans a week. Caffeine: no more than 200 mg a day. Alcohol: no known safe level, so avoid it (NG201 1.3.10).

test.q: What is the maximum daily caffeine intake advised in pregnancy?
options: 100 mg
200 mg
300 mg
400 mg
test.why: NHS advice: no more than 200 mg of caffeine a day in pregnancy, as higher intake is linked to miscarriage and stillbirth.

whyNot.0: 100 mg is about one mug of instant coffee, below the limit.
whyNot.3: 400 mg is double the recommended limit.
